assessment.title: Final assessment — Discovering the discipline
assessment.description: Analyse a proposed workplace intervention by distinguishing psychological claims, scientific questions, relevant fields, professional titles and ethical requirements.
assessment.instructions:
## Instructions
1. Read the NovaWork case and separate observed facts, interpretations and claims that require evidence.
2. Formulate two testable psychological questions and propose at least one observable indicator for each.
3. Use at least three different fields or levels of explanation and justify how they complement one another.
4. Distinguish the possible roles of an occupational psychologist, clinical psychologist, psychiatrist and psychotherapist without assuming competence from a title alone.
5. Identify at least five ethical or professional issues, including purpose, information, consent, confidentiality, competence and referral.
6. Propose a cautious action plan that states the missing information, required checks and limits of the conclusion.

## NovaWork case
NovaWork employs 120 people. Following an increase in absence, management buys an application advertised as “validated by neuroscience”. A ten-item questionnaire classifies each employee as motivated, fragile or resilient. The provider claims it can identify future sickness absence with 95% accuracy but supplies no study and does not describe the population on which the tool was evaluated. Participation is described as voluntary, yet team leaders publicly remind people who have not responded. The notice calls the results anonymous, but management requests individual scores to decide work assignments. The provider calls himself a “psycho-expert and analyst” without naming a protected title or verifiable qualification. An employee reports panic attacks and asks whether the provider can prescribe treatment. Management intends to launch the system the following week and asks you for a reasoned opinion.

## Submission format
A structured 900–1,200 word report using the six required sections and citing resources from the stage.

## Remediation
For every criterion below 70%, revisit the corresponding concepts, revise that part while identifying the changes, and submit a new version. Keep the sources and state any remaining limits.

requirements: Facts, interpretations and claims are distinguished.
Two testable questions and their indicators are formulated.
The accuracy claim is treated as a claim requiring verification.
At least three fields or levels are used accurately.
Their relevance and complementarity are justified.
No field is presented as a complete explanation by default.
Professional titles and roles are distinguished without extrapolation.
The provider’s qualifications are identified as requiring verification.
The request for medication and the panic attacks lead to an appropriate and cautious referral.

rubric.criterion: Ethical analysis and protection of people
requirements: Purpose, information, consent, confidentiality, competence and power are analysed.
The conflict between anonymity and individual scores is explicit.
The proposals concretely reduce risks to employees.
The response is structured, evidence-based and understandable.
Missing information and limits are stated.
The action plan does not promise an unsupported outcome.

lessons.title: Defining psychology
lessons.summary: Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. This lesson establishes a rigorous definition of the discipline, distinguishes direct observation from inference, and explains why psychological claims must be tested against evidence.
objectives: Define psychology as a scientific discipline.
Distinguish observable behaviour from a mental process.
Turn a broad question about people into an empirically testable question.
Explain why intuition and personal experience are not enough to establish psychological knowledge.

content.text: Psychology is not limited to psychotherapy or the study of mental disorders. It investigates how people and, depending on the question, other animals perceive, learn, remember, feel, decide and act. Some research primarily develops fundamental knowledge; other work applies that knowledge in health, education, employment or ergonomics.

Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Behaviour is an activity that can be observed or measured. A mental process includes perception, thought, emotion, memory or decision-making. It is not always directly observable, but it can be studied through indicators defined in advance.

Saying that someone “lacks motivation” is too vague to count as a scientific observation. A study could instead measure how long the person works on a task, how many attempts they make after failure, and their responses on a validated motivation scale. The abstract concept is then connected to explicit observations without being reduced to a single measure.

Scientific describes a way of working: formulating a precise question, proposing a testable explanation, collecting data systematically, and accepting that conclusions may be corrected by new observations. A single study does not establish a final truth. Findings become more robust when other researchers examine and replicate them and when they are considered alongside the wider body of evidence.

Key point: psychology studies behaviour and mental processes; it uses observations and measurements; it does not read minds; and psychological claims must be open to discussion using evidence rather than intuition alone.

lessons.title: The major fields of psychology
lessons.summary: Psychology includes fields that differ in their questions, levels of analysis and settings of application. This lesson shows how several perspectives can be relevant to the same phenomenon without reducing the discipline to clinical psychology or forcing every situation into a single field.
objectives: Identify the characteristic questions of several major fields of psychology.
Distinguish a field of research, a level of explanation and a professional setting.
Use biological, cognitive, developmental and social perspectives to analyse the same situation.
Distinguish the production of fundamental knowledge from the application of psychological knowledge.
prerequisites: Define psychology as the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes.
Distinguish observable behaviour, mental processes and indicators.

content.text: Psychology is not a single, uniform field. Its areas develop around different questions, populations, levels of analysis and settings. Cognitive psychology studies attention, memory, language and reasoning; developmental psychology examines change across the lifespan; social psychology investigates the influence of other people and groups; and biopsychology connects biological functioning with behaviour. This map is useful, but it is neither exhaustive nor made of rigid boundaries.

A field is a set of questions and methods, whereas a level of explanation describes the angle from which a phenomenon is studied. To explain difficulty concentrating, researchers might examine sleep and biological functioning, attentional mechanisms, developmental change or the influence of the social environment. These explanations may complement one another when they concern distinct mechanisms.

Invented example: a student repeatedly postpones her work. A cognitive approach might examine working memory and attentional control; a developmental approach, the development of self-regulation; a social approach, group norms and comparison with peers; and a health approach, sleep and stress. Naming several fields does not remove the need to formulate testable hypotheses and collect evidence.

The distinction between fundamental research and application concerns the immediate purpose of the work, not a hierarchy of value. Fundamental research primarily seeks to understand a mechanism. Applied work uses or evaluates knowledge in health, education, employment, justice or other settings. The same field can combine research and practice: clinical, occupational and health psychology also produce knowledge, while cognitive or social findings can guide interventions.

Common misconception: psychology and psychotherapy are not the same thing. Clinical psychology is important, but the discipline also studies the brain and behaviour, perception, learning, development, personality, social relationships, health, education, work and many other topics. To place a question, first ask what phenomenon is being studied, at what level, and for what purpose.

lessons.title: Professions and ethics
lessons.summary: In France, the titles psychologist, psychiatrist and psychotherapist and the description psychoanalyst do not imply the same training or scope of practice. This lesson explains the French framework and shows how competence, informed consent, confidentiality, rights and referral support responsible practice.
objectives: Distinguish the titles psychologist, psychiatrist and psychotherapist and the description psychoanalyst in France.
Identify the limits of a practitioner’s competence and situations that require referral.
Analyse a situation using consent, confidentiality, respect for the person and protection from abuse of power.
Distinguish legal requirements, professional rules and context-sensitive ethical decisions.
prerequisites: Define psychology as a scientific discipline.
Distinguish a field of research, a level of explanation and a setting of application.

content.text: In France, professional use of the title psychologist is protected by law and depends on specified qualifications or authorisations. A psychiatrist is a specialist physician who can make a medical diagnosis and prescribe medication. Holding the title psychologist does not in itself make someone a physician and does not authorise medication prescribing. Both professions may work in care, research, teaching or other settings depending on their training and role.

Use of the title psychotherapist is also regulated and requires registration; it is not interchangeable with psychologist or the medical specialty of psychiatry. Someone describing themselves as a psychoanalyst may also be a psychologist or psychiatrist, but this is not automatic. Each protected title, relevant qualification, registration, advertised method and actual scope of competence must therefore be checked separately.

Invented example: an occupational psychologist meets an employee who reports panic attacks and an immediate risk to her safety. The psychologist can listen, assess the situation within the limits of her role, and refer the employee to appropriate services. She must not imply that occupational training automatically covers every clinical or medical intervention. Recognising limits and arranging a referral are parts of competent practice.

Professional ethics organise responsibility towards people. The 2021 French code emphasises rights and dignity, autonomy, information, privacy, professional secrecy and confidentiality. These principles require practitioners to explain the purpose and framework of an intervention, seek free and informed consent, protect information, and limit sharing to what is justified. Applicable legal duties remain binding and must be assessed in context.

A professional title does not guarantee universal competence or the quality of a particular intervention. Before placing trust in a service, ask for the exact title, relevant training, confidentiality framework, purpose and limits, consent arrangements, and referral options. Refusing to explain the framework, guaranteeing outcomes, pressuring someone to continue, or requesting information without a clear purpose are warning signs.

assessment.title: Final assessment — Understanding the major schools
assessment.description: Compare several psychological explanations of the same situation without turning schools into labels, specifying for each the proposed mechanism, predictions, necessary data, historical contribution and limitations.
assessment.instructions:
## Instructions
1. Read the CampusLang case and separate observed behaviour, Maya’s statements and the interpretations proposed by the team.
2. Formulate a behaviorist analysis including at least one operant contingency and, if relevant, a classical-conditioning hypothesis.
3. Formulate a cognitive analysis with a bounded mechanism, a possible manipulation, a measure and a result that would contradict the hypothesis.
4. Present what a humanistic perspective would seek to understand about Maya’s experience and goals without treating a value as evidence of effectiveness.
5. Present a cautious psychodynamic hypothesis, then explain what makes it difficult to test and what data could at least make it more precise.
6. Compare the four perspectives in a mechanism-prediction-data-limitation table and propose an integrated explanation that does not exceed the available information.
7. Cite at least four resources from the stage, including one primary historical source, and explicitly distinguish historical citation from contemporary evidence.

## CampusLang case
CampusLang offers an optional language-learning app. Maya, a first-year student, has used it every evening for six weeks. At first, she mainly studied when the app displayed a streak and awarded badges. She now says she feels tense whenever she hears the reminder sound, even on days when she planned to rest. She answers familiar exercises very quickly but fails when an instruction changes slightly. In an interview, she explains that she wants to speak with her grandmother in her first language but feels ashamed of making mistakes in front of others. One teacher claims that everything is explained by the app’s rewards. A colleague argues that Maya simply lacks self-confidence. Another contributor mentions an unconscious conflict linked to family expectations without asking further questions. The team wants to increase the number of reminders and asks which explanation should be retained. No prior measurement, comparison group or clinical information is available.

## Submission format
A structured 1,200–1,500 word report including a comparative table and an integrated conclusion.

## Remediation
For each criterion below 70%, revisit the associated concepts and rewrite only the insufficient sections. The revised version must add one falsifiable prediction, one missing datum and one limitation for each relevant perspective while retaining the first version for comparison.

requirements: The schools are defined without major anachronism.
Classical conditioning, operant conditioning and reinforcement are used correctly.
Historical psychoanalysis and later psychodynamic approaches are not conflated.
Each perspective includes an explicitly stated mechanism.
The behaviorist and cognitive analyses generate observable predictions.
The proposals are not mere restatements of the behaviour.
Missing data and alternative explanations are identified.
At least one result capable of contradicting each testable hypothesis is stated.
Historical influence, plausibility and empirical support are distinguished.
The table compares perspectives using the same dimensions.
The conclusion combines relevant levels without declaring the schools equivalent.
The recommendation about reminders remains proportionate to the data and considers adverse effects.
At least four stage resources are cited precisely.
A primary historical source is presented as such.
The text is structured, nuanced and follows the requested format.

lessons.title: The birth of experimental psychology
lessons.summary: Experimental psychology emerged gradually at the intersection of philosophy, physiology and new measurement practices. This lesson uses the Leipzig laboratory as an institutional landmark, distinguishes experimentation from free introspection, and compares structuralism with functionalism without reducing the history of the discipline to a linear succession of founders.
objectives: Explain why 1879 is an institutional landmark rather than the instant birth of psychology.
Identify what experimentation and measurement changed in the study of psychological processes.
Distinguish structuralism and functionalism through their main questions.
Identify a historical simplification and formulate a more nuanced account.
prerequisites: Define psychology as the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes.

content.text: During the nineteenth century, questions about the mind did not suddenly leave philosophy and become scientific. Work in physiology, psychophysics and reaction-time measurement gradually made some phenomena accessible to controlled observation. Wilhelm Wundt’s creation of a laboratory in Leipzig in 1879 is often used as a landmark because it embodied a lasting organisation of research and training. This landmark means neither that no psychological experiment existed before it nor that one person created the entire discipline.

An experimental approach varies or controls conditions in order to observe their effects on a defined response. Early laboratories could present a sound or a light, measure reaction time and compare repeated conditions. Reports of conscious experience could also be collected, but under regulated conditions; they were not equivalent to free, unverifiable self-observation.

In a simple task, a person presses a button when a light appears. The researcher defines the stimulus, records the delay in milliseconds, repeats the trials and compares, for example, a predictable condition with an unpredictable one. Reaction time does not directly reveal the person’s entire thought process, but it provides a public and reproducible indicator of a bounded process.

Structuralism, especially associated with Edward Titchener, sought to describe the elements of conscious experience. Functionalism, associated in particular with William James, instead asked what mental activities are for and how they contribute to adaptation. Both orientations used introspection, but for different purposes and alongside other observations. Treating Wundt as wholly equivalent to Titchener’s later structuralism erases important historical differences.

Key point: a discipline is built through institutions, instruments, methods and debates. Landmarks such as Leipzig in 1879 are useful provided that history is not turned into a story about a single inventor, a single method or an inevitable progression towards current views.

lessons.title: Behaviorism and learning
lessons.summary: Behaviorism strengthened the controlled study of relations between the environment and behaviour. This lesson distinguishes its methodological project from learning mechanisms, then compares classical and operant conditioning while avoiding confusion between reinforcement, punishment, positive and negative.
objectives: Explain the methodological project of behaviorism and its historical context.
Represent classical conditioning with its stimuli and responses.
Analyse operant conditioning through a behaviour and its consequence.
Distinguish the experimental contribution, scope and limitations of a behaviorist explanation.
prerequisites: Distinguish observable behaviour from a mental process.
Understand the role of a measurement and an experimental condition.

content.text: At the beginning of the twentieth century, John B. Watson advocated a psychology centred on observable behaviour and relations between stimuli and responses. This project rejected private mental states as an indispensable basis for scientific explanation. It favoured operational definitions, controlled protocols and public predictions. Behaviorism was not a single doctrine, however: the positions of Watson, Skinner and contemporary learning research are not interchangeable.

In classical conditioning, an organism learns a relation between events. A stimulus that was initially neutral, when repeatedly paired with a stimulus that already elicits a response, may eventually trigger a conditioned response. The mechanism primarily concerns the predictive value of stimuli; it does not assume that the person voluntarily decides to produce the response.

In operant conditioning, the future probability of a behaviour varies according to its consequences. Reinforcement increases the behaviour; punishment decreases it. Positive means that an event is added and negative that it is removed. Negative reinforcement is therefore not punishment: it increases a behaviour because an aversive event disappears.

A revision app immediately congratulates a user after ten minutes of work and awards a point. If session frequency increases, the point or praise functions as positive reinforcement. If the user studies to stop an unpleasant alert and this strategy increases, removal of the alert may function as negative reinforcement. The category depends on the observed effect on behaviour, not the designer’s intention or whether the consequence seems morally pleasant.

Key point: behaviorist approaches produced powerful methods for studying learning and changing defined behaviours. On their own, they do not explain all human learning, especially when expectations, memory, observation of others, goals or social context alter behaviour. A useful explanation therefore states what the model predicts and what it leaves outside its scope.

lessons.title: Cognitivism, humanism and psychoanalysis
lessons.summary: Contemporary psychology inherited traditions that neither ask the same questions nor apply the same standards of evidence. This lesson presents the cognitive revolution, the humanistic approach and the psychoanalytic or psychodynamic tradition while distinguishing historical contribution, concepts, testable predictions and empirical scope.
objectives: Explain how the cognitive revolution made mental processes compatible with experimental study.
Present the central questions of the humanistic approach without treating its values as demonstrated findings.
Distinguish historical Freudian psychoanalysis from later psychodynamic approaches.
Compare several traditions through their mechanisms, predictions and levels of evidence.
prerequisites: Distinguish observable behaviour from a mental process.
Understand the behaviorist project and the principles of conditioning.

content.text: From the 1950s, work in psychology, linguistics, computer science and neuroscience renewed the study of memory, language, attention and problem solving. The cognitive revolution was not simply a return to free introspection: it built information-processing models and tested them against observable responses, errors, reaction times and recall performance. A mental process can therefore be theorised without being treated as directly visible.

Two people obtain the same score on a memory task, but one answers quickly with some errors while the other answers slowly without errors. A cognitive model can propose different strategies, then predict how performance will change if the delay, load or instruction varies. The model is useful if it produces predictions that could fail, not merely if it tells a plausible story after the event.

The humanistic approach developed in reaction to views of behaviour and personality considered overly deterministic. It emphasises lived experience, meaning, choice, relationships and personal growth. Carl Rogers notably emphasised a person-centred relationship. These orientations influenced clinical practice and ideas about the therapeutic alliance, but their values, personality models and the effects of an intervention must be evaluated separately.

Freudian psychoanalysis proposes that unconscious conflicts and processes contribute to behaviour and personality. Its historical influence on psychotherapy, culture and attention to personal history is substantial. Several classical propositions are nevertheless difficult to falsify or have received limited direct support. Later psychodynamic approaches changed concepts, duration and methods; evaluating them requires distinguishing a general theory, a precise mechanism and the effectiveness of a defined intervention.

Key point: comparing traditions means neither choosing a school as an identity nor declaring them equally supported. For the same case, specify the question, proposed mechanism, expected observations, alternative explanations and available level of evidence. Ideas from different traditions can be reformulated and tested without validating their entire historical system.

concepts.title: The cognitive revolution
concepts.description: The cognitive revolution restored the study of representations and mental processes through models that generate observable predictions.

concepts.title: The humanistic perspective
concepts.description: The humanistic approach emphasises lived experience, meaning, relationships and capacity for growth while requiring values to be distinguished from empirical claims.

concepts.title: Psychoanalysis and psychodynamic approaches
concepts.description: Historical psychoanalysis and psychodynamic approaches give a role to unconscious processes and relational history, but their propositions and interventions must be evaluated separately.

tasks.description: Using the humanistic section, create three columns: value or priority, proposition about human functioning, and observation needed to evaluate it.

tasks.title: Compare four explanations of the same case
tasks.description: For a person postponing an important task, formulate a behaviorist, cognitive, humanistic and psychodynamic hypothesis; for each, state one prediction, one useful datum and one limitation.

assessmentBanks.assessmentTitle: Concept check — The subject matter of psychology

questions.prompt: Which definition best describes scientific psychology?
questions.explanation: Psychology studies behaviour and mental processes through explicit questions and evidence.

options.label: The scientific study of behaviour and mental processes
The exclusive study of the brain

questions.prompt: Which topics can psychology study?
questions.explanation: The discipline studies observable behaviour as well as processes such as memory, emotion and perception.

questions.prompt: Psychology is limited to therapeutic support.
questions.explanation: Clinical practice is one part of a discipline that also includes fundamental research and many applications.

questions.prompt: Which is clearly a psychological research question?
questions.explanation: The influence of social context on decisions concerns measurable behaviour and mental processes.

options.label: How does the presence of other people affect a decision?
What is the atomic mass of carbon?
Which planet is closest to the Sun?

questions.prompt: Psychology can produce fundamental knowledge and practical applications.
questions.explanation: Psychology connects the study of mechanisms with uses in health, education, work and other settings.

assessmentBanks.assessmentTitle: Concept check — Behaviour and mental processes

questions.prompt: Which is directly observable behaviour?
questions.explanation: Raising a hand is observable, while remembering, feeling and intending are mental processes inferred from indicators.

questions.prompt: Why are indicators used to study a mental process?
questions.explanation: A mental process is not always directly observable, so defined measures support cautious inference.

options.label: Because the process is not always directly observable
Because an indicator always proves causation

questions.prompt: Reaction time is the mental process itself.
questions.explanation: Reaction time is an observable indicator; it is not identical to the process being studied.

questions.prompt: Which measures could indicate attention?
questions.explanation: Response time and errors are observable measures; vague labels without criteria are not.

options.label: The statement “they are inattentive” without a criterion

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is the most cautious?
questions.explanation: A measure supports a bounded interpretation; it does not reveal a person’s mind directly.

options.label: These results are consistent with lower attention on this task.
We know exactly what the person is thinking.
One error reveals the whole personality.
The indicator rules out every alternative explanation.

questions.prompt: Which question is most directly testable?
questions.explanation: It specifies a measurable condition and an observable result.

options.label: Does a shorter night of sleep increase errors on this task?
Does sleep possess a beneficial essence?
Why are some people simply better?

questions.prompt: Which features belong to empirical inquiry?
questions.explanation: Empirical inquiry uses systematic observation, explicit measures and revisable conclusions.

questions.prompt: One personal experience is enough to establish a general pattern.
questions.explanation: Experience may suggest a question, but general conclusions require systematically collected evidence.

questions.prompt: What should researchers do when robust results contradict their original hypothesis?
questions.explanation: Scientific explanations must be revised or rejected when evidence does not support them.

options.label: Revise the explanation and examine the method
Replace the data with an anecdote

questions.prompt: Replication and scrutiny by other researchers can strengthen or correct a conclusion.
questions.explanation: New observations and criticism make scientific knowledge cumulative and revisable.

questions.prompt: Which field primarily studies psychological change across the lifespan?
questions.explanation: Developmental psychology studies change and continuity at different ages.

questions.prompt: Which question most directly belongs to cognitive psychology?
questions.explanation: Cognitive psychology studies attention, memory, language and reasoning.

options.label: How does attention affect recall of a word list?
How should a team schedule be organised?
How does average population height change?
Which law regulates a professional title?

questions.prompt: Which statements about fields of psychology are accurate?
questions.explanation: Fields can overlap and differ in their questions, methods or settings; an introductory list is not exhaustive.

options.label: They can differ in questions and methods.
Every situation belongs to exactly one field.
A list of fields is always final.

questions.prompt: Clinical psychology represents the whole of psychology.
questions.explanation: Clinical psychology is one field among many fundamental and applied areas.

questions.prompt: What is the best criterion for placing a new question within a field?
questions.explanation: Start with the phenomenon, question and level of analysis rather than a keyword.

options.label: The precise object and research question

questions.prompt: Which question mainly uses a social level of explanation?
questions.explanation: The effect of group norms on behaviour is a social-psychological question.

options.label: How do group norms influence risk-taking?
How does the ability change between ages 6 and 12?

questions.prompt: Which question mainly uses a biological level of explanation?
questions.explanation: Measures of neural or physiological mechanisms mainly concern a biological level.

options.label: Which brain networks are active during the task?
Which expectations does the group communicate?
How does this ability change with age?

questions.prompt: Why can several levels of explanation be relevant to one behaviour?
questions.explanation: They can address different mechanisms and support complementary hypotheses, all of which still require evidence.

options.label: They prove that evidence is unnecessary.
They guarantee that every explanation is true.

questions.prompt: A brain-based explanation automatically makes cognitive or social explanations unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Different levels may answer different questions and can complement one another.

questions.prompt: After proposing four levels of explanation for procrastination, what comes next scientifically?
questions.explanation: The perspectives must become testable hypotheses linked to relevant evidence.

options.label: Formulate testable hypotheses and define the required evidence
Choose the explanation that feels most intuitive

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes fundamental research?
questions.explanation: Its immediate purpose is to understand a mechanism or pattern, even if applications may follow.

options.label: Studying how attention selects competing information
Choosing a slogan without evaluating it

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes applied work?
questions.explanation: Applied work uses or evaluates knowledge in a concrete setting.

options.label: Evaluating a workplace change intended to reduce errors
Only describing the history of a concept

questions.prompt: Which statements about research and application are correct?
questions.explanation: A field may create and apply knowledge, and applications can be evaluated empirically.

options.label: One field can combine research and practice.
An application can be evaluated scientifically.
Fundamental research can never become useful.

questions.prompt: “Applied” means that scientific methods are no longer necessary.
questions.explanation: Applications also need clear objectives, outcome measures and acknowledged limits.

questions.prompt: An occupational psychologist tests whether a new organisation reduces errors. Which description is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Applied work and empirical evaluation can occur together.

options.label: Application and empirical evaluation can be combined.
It cannot be psychology because it occurs at work.

assessmentBanks.assessmentTitle: Concept check — Professional titles and roles

questions.prompt: In France, who is necessarily a physician by virtue of their title?
questions.explanation: A psychiatrist is a specialist physician. The title psychologist is not a medical title.

questions.prompt: A psychologist can prescribe medication solely by virtue of the title psychologist.
questions.explanation: A psychologist is not a physician solely by virtue of that title and cannot prescribe medication on that basis.

questions.prompt: Which titles discussed in this lesson are governed by specific French legal frameworks?
questions.explanation: Psychologist and psychotherapist are regulated by distinct texts; psychiatrist is a medical specialty.

questions.prompt: Calling oneself a psychoanalyst automatically proves that the person is also a psychologist or psychiatrist.
questions.explanation: A psychoanalyst may hold either title, but this must be checked separately.

questions.prompt: What is the most reliable response to a professional description?
questions.explanation: Check the exact title, training, relevant registration and scope of competence separately.

options.label: Check title, training, registration and competence separately
Rely only on popularity on social media

questions.prompt: A practitioner encounters a situation outside their training. What is the most responsible response?
questions.explanation: They should explain their limits and arrange an appropriate referral rather than claim universal competence.

options.label: Acknowledge the limit and suggest an appropriate referral
Avoid giving the person any explanation

questions.prompt: Holding the title psychologist means being competent in every specialty of psychology.
questions.explanation: A title does not replace the training and experience required for a particular intervention.

questions.prompt: Which information helps assess whether an intervention falls within a practitioner’s competence?
questions.explanation: Relevant training, experience, role and the nature of the need are more informative than a general label.

options.label: The nature and urgency of the need

questions.prompt: Why can referral to another professional demonstrate competence?
questions.explanation: It shows that the practitioner recognises the limits of their role and seeks an appropriate response.

options.label: It protects the person and respects professional limits
It proves the first practitioner knows nothing
It removes the need for consent

questions.prompt: What takes priority when a person faces an immediate safety risk?
questions.explanation: The urgency must be assessed and appropriate services involved under the relevant professional and legal framework.

options.label: Assess the urgency and involve appropriate services
Wait for the next appointment without acting
Publish the situation to ask for advice
Promise absolute secrecy without examining the framework

questions.prompt: What should be clarified before a psychological intervention?
questions.explanation: People need understandable information about purpose, framework, information use and relevant limits.

options.label: An obligation to accept without questions

questions.prompt: A company requests individual scores from a questionnaire presented as anonymous. What is the first problem?
questions.explanation: Individual disclosure contradicts the promise of anonymity; purpose, consent and access must be clarified.

options.label: The contradiction between promised anonymity and individual disclosure
The questionnaire must be too short
The results should be published online

questions.prompt: Consent is valid even when the person does not know the purpose or use of their data.
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires understandable information about purpose, framework and relevant consequences.

questions.prompt: Which practices support confidentiality?
questions.explanation: Limiting collection and access, explaining the rules and sharing only justified information reduce privacy risks.

options.label: Share the whole record by default

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between professional ethics and law?
questions.explanation: Ethical reflection guides practice, while applicable legal duties must also be identified and followed.

options.label: Professional ethics guide practice without replacing legal duties.
A professional code overrides every law.
Ethics and law are unrelated to practice.

questions.prompt: Why is 1879 often used as a landmark in the history of psychology?
questions.explanation: The Leipzig laboratory is a lasting institutional landmark for research and training, not an absolute beginning.

options.label: Wundt established a lasting laboratory for psychological research there
All reflection on the mind began that year
The first physiological measurement was made that year
All schools of psychology were founded simultaneously

questions.prompt: The 1879 landmark proves that no psychology-related experiment existed before then.
questions.explanation: Work in physiology, psychophysics and measurement preceded the Leipzig laboratory.

questions.prompt: Which elements contribute to the institutionalisation of a scientific discipline?
questions.explanation: Laboratories, instruments, training and publications make a scientific community and its methods durable.

options.label: The isolated opinion of one founder

questions.prompt: Which historical statement is the most cautious?
questions.explanation: A rigorous history uses landmarks without attributing the whole discipline to one person or date.

options.label: The Leipzig laboratory is one major landmark among several transformations
Psychology immediately became identical in every country

questions.prompt: In which city did Wundt organise the laboratory used as the 1879 landmark?
questions.explanation: The laboratory was located in Leipzig, Germany.

questions.prompt: What makes a reaction time scientifically useful?
questions.explanation: It is a defined measurement that can be recorded and compared across explicit conditions.

options.label: It can be measured and compared according to a protocol

questions.prompt: What must a simple reaction-time experiment specify?
questions.explanation: The stimulus, response, measurement and comparison conditions make the protocol interpretable.

questions.prompt: Wundt defended only free self-observation without experimental control.
questions.explanation: His writings instead connect psychological observation to controlled experimental conditions.

questions.prompt: A predictable condition produces a shorter mean time than an unpredictable condition. Which conclusion is warranted?
questions.explanation: The result concerns the observed difference in this protocol; it does not describe all mental activity.

options.label: Predictability is associated with a faster response in this protocol
All mental processes are now explained

questions.prompt: What is the delay between the appearance of a stimulus and the recorded response called?
questions.explanation: This delay is reaction time.

questions.prompt: Which question best corresponds to functionalism?
questions.explanation: Functionalism examines the usefulness and adaptive function of mental activity and behaviour.

options.label: What purpose does this mental activity serve in adaptation?
Which elements exactly compose this conscious experience?
Which brain structure is sufficient to explain everything?

questions.prompt: Who is structuralism mainly associated with in this lesson?
questions.explanation: Systematic structuralism is mainly associated with Edward Titchener; equating it entirely with Wundt is reductive.

questions.prompt: Structuralists and functionalists always used completely opposing methods.
questions.explanation: They differed mainly in their questions and aims; both used introspection, among other methods.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe the two orientations?
questions.explanation: Structuralism concerns the composition of experience and functionalism its adaptive functions.

options.label: Structuralism analyses the contents of experience
Functionalism studies the usefulness of mental activity

questions.prompt: Which school is notably associated with William James?
questions.explanation: William James is a major figure in functionalism.

questions.prompt: Which objective does Watson place at the forefront of his manifesto?
questions.explanation: Watson presents an objective psychology aimed in particular at predicting and controlling behaviour.

questions.prompt: All authors described as behaviorists defend exactly the same theory.
questions.explanation: The term covers several historical and theoretical positions; Watson and Skinner are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Which elements correspond to the behaviorist methodological project?
questions.explanation: The approach favours measurable behaviour, public conditions and testable predictions.

options.label: Treat every private experience as sufficient evidence

questions.prompt: Which limitation should accompany a strictly behaviorist explanation?
questions.explanation: An analysis centred on contingencies may leave out relevant cognitive, social or biological processes.

options.label: It may omit internal processes and social context

questions.prompt: Which psychologist published Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It in 1913?
questions.explanation: It was John B. Watson.

questions.prompt: In classical conditioning, what does the organism mainly learn?
questions.explanation: It learns that one stimulus predicts another, which changes the response to the first.

options.label: A consequence following a voluntary action

questions.prompt: A conditioned response must necessarily be chosen voluntarily.
questions.explanation: Classical conditioning often concerns elicited responses that do not require a voluntary decision.

questions.prompt: After repeated pairings, a previously neutral sound elicits salivation. What has the sound become?
questions.explanation: The sound has become a conditioned stimulus capable of eliciting a conditioned response.

questions.prompt: Which elements must be identified in a complete classical-conditioning diagram?
questions.explanation: The diagram distinguishes stimuli and responses before and after learning.

questions.prompt: What is the initial phase during which the conditioned association forms called?
questions.explanation: This phase is acquisition.

questions.prompt: What effect defines reinforcement?
questions.explanation: Reinforcement increases the future probability of the behaviour it follows.

options.label: The person judges the consequence pleasant

questions.prompt: An alarm stops when a person fastens a seat belt, increasing seat-belt use. What is this?
questions.explanation: Removing the alarm increases the behaviour: this is negative reinforcement.

questions.prompt: In operant terminology, negative means bad or harmful.
questions.explanation: Negative indicates removal of an event; it is not a moral judgement.

questions.prompt: What information is needed to classify an operant consequence?
questions.explanation: You must determine what is added or removed and observe whether behaviour increases or decreases.

options.label: Is an event added or removed?
Does the behaviour increase or decrease?
Does the consequence seem morally good?

questions.prompt: What is the successive reinforcement of approximations towards a target behaviour called?
questions.explanation: This procedure is shaping.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a scientific cognitive explanation from a plausible story told after the event?
questions.explanation: A scientific model makes observable predictions that can be contradicted.

questions.prompt: Which measurements can test a cognitive model?
questions.explanation: Time, errors and recall are observable indicators that allow the model to be compared with data.

questions.prompt: The cognitive revolution made observable behaviour unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Cognitive models are tested precisely through observable responses and performance.

questions.prompt: Which context contributed to the cognitive revolution?
questions.explanation: Developments in linguistics, computer science, neuroscience and psychology renewed the study of the mind.

options.label: Exchange among several disciplines in the 1950s
The disappearance of memory as a subject
An exclusive return to ancient philosophy

questions.prompt: What is the movement that restored the scientific study of mental processes to a central place from the 1950s called?
questions.explanation: It is the cognitive revolution.

questions.prompt: Which theme is central to the humanistic approach?
questions.explanation: Lived experience, meaning, relationships and potential for growth occupy a central place.

options.label: Explaining every behaviour through one gene

questions.prompt: A humanistic value and a claim about therapeutic effectiveness are validated in exactly the same way.
questions.explanation: A value guides practice; a claim about effects requires a defined empirical evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which psychologist is most associated with the person-centred approach?
questions.explanation: Carl Rogers developed the person-centred approach.

questions.prompt: What must be distinguished when evaluating a humanistic proposition?
questions.explanation: Clarity requires separating values, theoretical models and observable effects of an intervention.

options.label: The idea that all claims are equivalent

questions.prompt: Which humanistic psychologist is associated with the hierarchy of needs and self-actualisation?
questions.explanation: It is Abraham Maslow.

assessmentBanks.assessmentTitle: Concept check — Psychoanalysis and psychodynamic approaches

questions.prompt: Which distinction is most important when evaluating the psychodynamic tradition?
questions.explanation: A historical theory, a precise mechanism and a defined intervention do not automatically have the same support.

options.label: Distinguish the historical system, mechanism and intervention
Confuse cultural influence with experimental evidence

questions.prompt: The historical influence of a theory is sufficient to demonstrate all its propositions.
questions.explanation: Historical influence and empirical support are distinct questions.

questions.prompt: Which themes belong to the psychoanalytic or psychodynamic tradition?
questions.explanation: This tradition notably emphasises unconscious processes, conflicts and relational history.

questions.prompt: Why are some classical Freudian propositions difficult to evaluate scientifically?
questions.explanation: They may be framed so that they explain opposing results without a clear observation capable of refuting them.

options.label: They sometimes lack explicit falsification criteria
They always use measurements that are too precise

questions.prompt: What term describes the possibility that a proposition can be contradicted by an observation?
questions.explanation: It is falsifiability, or refutability.
